A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from TALE to SAGE. All 29 pages of v2 and 26 pages of v3, including appendices, equations, prompts, figures and tables, support comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying the changes.

before.justification: v2 reports original QA experiments, human annotations, component ablations, prompt-sensitivity tests and failure analyses in Sections 4–5 and Appendices B–C.

after.justification: v3 retains original benchmark and human-evaluation results and reports additional RefGPT comparisons, search-engine experiments, Qwen evaluations, repeated runs and latency measurements.

M1.justification: The framework retains question-based initial queries, top-three search results, summarization, reflection, append-only memory and a binary final judgment. v3's unified query notation and memory-based judge signature restate the existing procedure and appendix prompts. Adaptive stopping and alternative domain tools remain future proposals.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate AmbigQA, HotpotQA, NQ-Open, TriviaQA and FreshQA on factual free-form QA. FreshQA already appears in v2 Section 4.2 and Appendix B.3. Additional FreshQA result rows expand reporting; Qwen and search-engine comparisons vary evaluator components on retained tasks.

E2.justification: v3 adds GPT-4-based RefGPT as the primary reference-based comparator, evaluates its human agreement in Table 1 and uses its labels for the main comparison in Table 2. EM, F1, unassisted judges, single-pass retrieval, self-consistency and multi-LLM voting are retained; the latter three already appeared in v2 Appendix C.1.

E3.justification: The primary quantitative comparison now measures verdict agreement with RefGPT, supplementing the retained human-based evaluation. Added designs compare single-pass, SAGE-1 and SAGE-3 across search engines, evaluate Qwen judges on GPT-4o candidates, and compare latency on 50 AmbigQA items. The main 300-instance samples and prompting budgets remain; newly identified dataset splits do not establish resampling.

E4.justification: v3 adds an explicit single-pass versus SAGE-1 comparison under the same query budget, search-engine robustness tests, a confusion-outcome distribution and numerical error-category frequencies. These strengthen component and failure analysis. Iteration, query-removal, prompt-sensitivity and topic-drift analyses were already present in v2, including its appendices.

E5.justification: v2 already states that rerunning the default prompt reproduced its results. v3 specifies two independent-day runs and tabulates their Macro-F1 values in Table 11, without establishing an increase over the earlier run count. Table 7 newly reports latency means and standard deviations; comparable uncertainty intervals are not added to the main accuracy or kappa results.

E6.justification: v3 adds RefGPT-agreement scores, expanded FreshQA entries, Qwen and search-engine results, confusion/error frequencies and latency measurements. Most retained human-agreement and prompt-ablation scores merely undergo rounding. Some carried-over entries change, including GPT-4o judging itself on AmbigQA from 0.590 in v2 Table 1 to 0.63 in v3 Table 9. Table 9's conflicting metric description prevents interpreting this as an established performance gain.

T1.justification: v3 numbers the module equations and expresses memory as an ordered sequence, consistent with v2's append-only trace and algorithm. The standard agreement and Macro-F1 formulas are retained. No new theorem, proof, substantive assumption or mathematical derivation is introduced.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains reference-free factual evaluation through iterative external evidence gathering with strong human agreement. v3 focuses its framing more explicitly on factual free-form QA and adds conclusion-level claims about robustness across search engines and the separate benefits of retrieval and reflection/refinement. It does not introduce a different central method.

C2.justification: v3 explicitly treats RefGPT as an imperfect proxy and distinguishes it from human evidence. Section 7 adds substantive boundaries concerning English-only validation, web-verifiable QA and binary verdicts. New interpretations attribute gains to evidence-sufficiency checking and discuss Qwen instruction-following thresholds. Existing context-window, source-credibility and judge-capability limitations are retained rather than newly introduced.

D1.justification: Appendix 8.1 newly specifies validation subsets and the December 18, 2024 FreshQA release, while Appendix 8.2 clarifies how memory supplies prompt inputs. v3 adds call and latency breakdowns and revised search-pricing assumptions, but omits v2's explicit input/output token totals and exact Mistral checkpoint link. The promise to release retrieved snippets remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v3 substantially reframes positioning around factual free-form QA and distinguishes short-answer verification from FActScore and newly cited SAFE's long-form fact evaluation. It adds QA-evaluation and judge-bias literature, including Wang et al., Kamalloo et al. and Gu et al., while removing the earlier WebGPT, SelfCheckGPT and Agent-as-a-Judge discussion. These are substantive positioning changes.

P1.justification: Beyond renaming TALE to SAGE, v3 extensively rewrites the introduction, consolidates the methodology, reorganizes the results, moves related work after the experiments and brings limitations into the main text. Appendix organization and explanatory prose are also extensively revised.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from one to two columns, redraws Figure 1 and adds the confusion-distribution figure. Human-agreement tables are merged and reorganized, the expanded raw-score table moves to the appendix, and search-engine, latency and repeated-run tables are added. Prompt panels and case-study tables are reformatted; the iteration plot is retained as Figure 3.

improvement.justification: The matched-query-budget comparison and search-engine tests strengthen evidence for the iterative design, while dataset-split disclosure and explicit applicability limits improve reproducibility and interpretation. The net gain is modest because the core human-evaluation evidence already existed. New reporting defects limit the improvement: Table 9 labels largely retained raw scores as RefGPT agreement, conflicting with Table 2, and the new error-category percentages total only 90%.
